en: To the north of the city of Saṃkāśya, there was a stūpa from the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, which had subsided into the underlying diamond-realm (vajra-maṇḍala).
When the Buddha descended from the heavens to preach the Dharma for his mother, he returned to this city. Ānanda asked:
"When a Buddha descends from heaven, what serves as his banner?
"I shall now manifest it through direct realization.
He then extended his hand downward and grasped the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha, bringing it forth.

This stūpa was constructed from various colored jade and stone; the stūpa was named Saṃghaśīrṣa, after the name of Kāśyapa Buddha’s father. It is said that the elder Vāyu built it out of compassion. It was three hundred cubits high and three and a half li square. Originally composed of the seven precious gems, it thus possessed seven colors. The city currently bears its name because of this very stūpa.
The reason why Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and others compiled the sūtras at this location was that there were two matters for which they could not have emerged from their place of parinirvāṇa:
first, because it was not among human beings;

and second, because when the fourfold assembly of devas and humans had come, they would all have been moved by grief and their minds would have become distracted, preventing them from listening with composure.
When the assembly had concluded, the kings built a saṃghārāma at that site, naming it the Kings’ Monastery (Rājaka-vihāra), located to the north of the stūpa.
Later, King Guṇaśrī found the stūpa obstructing the city gate; wishing to demolish it, he ordered the city to prepare hoes and axes, decreeing that it should be removed the following day.
At midnight, the stupa suddenly shifted and passed over the city wall; its sound shook the kingdom, and after traveling twenty li south of the city, it came to rest among the trees and groves.
As for the minister who advised the King to destroy the monasteries, his entire clan of five generations was executed.
Upon witnessing these omens, the King realized his error and reformed, becoming a lay devotee (*śraddhā-vatsala*).
It has been approximately forty years since he first moved here.

The various royal temples had fallen into ruin, but later a usurping king appeared who renovated and adorned them; they remain extant today. This is from the *Śuṣkavṛkṣa-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Withered Tree) spoken by the Buddha.
